Parlange, Ph.D., P.Eng., President DATE: April 4, 2024 SUBJECT: Discussion Item: Classification and Compensation Study Purpose of Submittal: Update the Committee on a recently launched classification and compensation study for URI’s non-classified staff.
Classified civil service positions, faculty, and graduate assistant positions will not be included as part of this review.
Points to Consider: URI is committed to fostering an inclusive, people -centered culture and continuing our efforts to attract, recognize, and retain outstanding staff and faculty.
In support of this strategic priority, we have recently launched a comprehensive review and revision of our classification and compensation structure for non- classified staff.
Huron Consulting Group was secured to support this study through a competitive Request for Proposal process.

Our goal is to develop a well -structured, transparent, and equitable compensation platform that provides clear pathways for advancement, rewards outstanding performance, and supports competitive compensation.
This modernization of our classification and compensation structure will result in a cohesive compensation philosophy, formal job architecture and career pathing, new job profiles more clearly connected to the competitive market, and policies and processes to sustain improvement.
The study is expected to take up to one year to complete.
Review and implementation of the study will be a multi- year effort, and we will work closely with the relevant staff and unions throughout the process.

Brief Fall 2020 Overview President Dooley shared that URI was purposeful in their decision-making process regarding Fall 2020 reopening.
The University conducted a thorough review of all possible reopening plans.
President Dooley stated that every decision was informed by CDC guidelines, the RI Department of Health, and on-campus health officials.
Deans, Faculty Senate, and Senior Leadership were heavily involved in these discussions and analyses as well.
Specifically, Qualitative Risk Analysis was used in this process.
Students’ and families’ opinions were heavily considered because the consensus was a strong desire to be back on campus rather than fully online.
This opinion was seen in national surveys across the country.
The University is currently planning to open the campus.

There will not be as many students living on campus as was traditionally seen in the past to reduce the risk of virus transmission.
URI pivoted and offered all summer sessions online, and it has been the highest summer enrollment ever recorded to date.
This summer, URI is investing in classroom technology to create the best teaching and learning environments for those classes offered remotely.
President Dooley shared that all of these plans are being discussed with an unknown budget.
The state is in a financial deficit, and it has impacted URI.
Another goal of URI is to keep its workforce

in place; but moving forward, this will depend on the monetary decisions from the federal government and state monies.
